title: LLM Cost Optimization and Model Routing: A Practical Guide for Engineering Leaders
summary: Calculate AI token cost, compare caching, batching and model routing, and connect engineering spend to completed work with Weave.
body_markdown:
## What is AI token cost?


AI token cost is the amount a model provider charges for processing input and generating output. The bill depends on the model, token counts, caching, and applicable service tier. A request can also incur tool or storage charges. Check the provider's current[OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing) ,[Anthropic](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing) , or[Gemini](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing) pricing before calculating a budget.


For engineering teams, the useful question is how much it costs to complete work at the required quality. A lower token bill is valuable when the code still passes its checks and the team can use it.


To optimize LLM cost, measure the full cost of a task first. Then test one change: reduce unnecessary context, reuse eligible prompt prefixes, batch work that can wait, or route suitable tasks to another model. Compare accepted results, retries, and latency alongside the bill.

## Build a cost baseline you can explain


Record the model, billable token categories, pricing date, owner, task, retries, and result. Keep coding subscriptions, metered API charges, and other infrastructure costs identifiable so the same expense is counted once.


For each token category, multiply its billable count by the applicable rate. If the rate is quoted per million tokens, divide the count by one million first. Add the resulting charges and any applicable non-token fees.


Provider billing categories differ:


Scroll horizontally if needed →


Provider Check in the current pricing documentation


[OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing) Model and service tier, input, cached input, cache writes where applicable, output, and tool charges.


[Anthropic](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing) Input, output, cache writes, cache reads, and cache duration.


[Gemini](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing) Model and processing mode, input, output, context caching, storage duration, and applicable tool charges.


Do not charge the same input tokens twice. For example,[OpenAI's caching documentation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching) distinguishes uncached-input, cached-input, and cache-write rates rather than adding a cache-write fee to the base rate. Reconcile your calculation with billing before using it to compare tools.


### How to calculate AI token cost


For a text workload with these billing categories, use:


**Token cost = (uncached input tokens × input rate + cache-write tokens × write rate + cache-read tokens × read rate + output tokens × output rate) ÷ 1,000,000.**


The rates in this formula are prices per million tokens. Split the token counts into the provider's mutually exclusive billing categories first. If your usage total already includes cached input, subtract the cached categories before applying the ordinary input rate. Add tool calls, storage, and other applicable charges separately.


The following is an **illustrative arithmetic example** , with invented rates and token counts. It is not a provider quote, customer result, or Weave benchmark.


Scroll horizontally if needed →


Billing category Billable tokens Illustrative rate × millions of tokens = cost


Uncached input 1,000,000 $2.00 × 1 = $2.00


Cache writes 500,000 $2.50 × 0.5 = $1.25


Cache reads 4,000,000 $0.20 × 4 = $0.80


Output 500,000 $10.00 × 0.5 = $5.00


**Total** **6,000,000** **$2.00 + $1.25 + $0.80 + $5.00 = $9.05**


This example assumes no tool, storage, or other fees. A single average token price would hide the difference between output, cache reads, and ordinary input. Use actual billed categories and the applicable model, context length, service tier, and pricing date when reproducing the calculation.


### Measure cost per accepted task


**Cost per accepted task = cost of all attempts in the workload ÷ number of accepted tasks.**


For example, if the hypothetical $9.05 workload above includes every attempt and produces eight accepted tasks, its token cost per accepted task is $9.05 ÷ 8, or about $1.13. Include spending on failed attempts in the numerator. Report human review time, infrastructure, and subscriptions separately unless you have included those costs in the calculation.


## Choose the control that fits the problem


Cost monitoring, model routing, and engineering measurement answer different questions. Use this checklist when evaluating a tool or building your own workflow.


Scroll horizontally if needed →


Decision Evidence to ask for What to check


Where is the bill growing? Spend by model, token category, and workload Coverage, pricing dates, and unallocated spend


Can this task use a cheaper model? The same tasks run under both routing policies Completion, retries, latency, and quality


Is the output acceptable? Tests, review results, reverts, and task acceptance A defined quality threshold and observation window


Which team owns the cost? Identity mapping and available tool billing data Shared accounts and missing attribution


Is spending producing useful work? Attributed cost and accepted output for the same cohort Comparable task mix, period, and denominator


### Compare the ways to reduce LLM cost


Choose the change that addresses the part of the bill you measured. The table below compares mechanisms and the evidence to collect; it does not promise a savings rate for your workload.


Scroll horizontally if needed →


Control When to test it What to verify before adopting it


Reduce unnecessary context Repeated files, retrieved passages, or history dominate input tokens Remove irrelevant material and check that task acceptance holds. Count any extra retrieval or follow-up calls.


Prompt caching Requests reuse a substantial, stable prefix Check model eligibility, actual cache hits, write prices, and retention.[OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching) requires matching prefixes;[Gemini](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching) documents model-specific caching requirements.


Batch processing Independent jobs can wait for asynchronous results Check supported models, expiration, and retry handling.[Anthropic's Message Batches API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing) offers discounted asynchronous processing; it is a different workflow from an interactive coding session.


Reduce unnecessary output Long responses or repeated explanations add output tokens Request the result format the task needs, then check for truncation, missing steps, and extra follow-up turns.


Model routing Tasks have different quality and reasoning requirements Compare the same tasks under both policies. Include routing charges, cache changes, escalation, failed runs, and latency.[Weave Router](https://weaveos.com/products/router) applies model routing to coding agents.


Provider billing and feature documentation was reviewed on October 16, 2026. Rates, eligibility, context thresholds, and processing modes can change. Check the linked source for the model and API you actually use.


## Evaluate routing and caching together


Model routing selects a model for a request. Prompt caching reuses eligible input context. Compare their combined cost on representative tasks: switching models can change cache reuse, while failed attempts can add requests and review work.


Start with a small evaluation set from the work your team actually does. Define success before testing a cheaper model: passing tests, accepted changes, required latency, or another task-specific result. Compare total cost across all attempts needed to reach that result. Include unsuccessful runs in the spending total.


Keep an escalation path for tasks that miss the threshold. Re-run the evaluation when models, prompts, pricing, or workload mix change. A published benchmark can inform a shortlist; your own acceptance results determine whether a routing policy fits your work.


## Connect spending to engineering output


Choose one cohort and time window, then review its costs, delivered work, and quality together. Keep unattributed spending visible. Recently merged code may need more time before defects or maintenance work appear.


Cost per merged PR can be useful for a consistent workload, but PR size and complexity vary. Review the underlying work alongside the ratio. Weave's[AI ROI methodology](https://weaveos.com/methodology/ai-roi) explains its output estimates and the distinction between observed cost efficiency and a financial return calculation.


## Common questions


**Will a cheaper model always reduce the cost of a task?**


Compare the full run. Extra attempts, cache changes, and human corrections can offset a lower rate. Measure cost per completed task alongside quality and latency.


**Can token counts prove AI ROI?**


Token counts describe consumption. A financial return calculation also needs attributable costs, a credible baseline, and a value for incremental benefits. Review[Weave's measurement methodology](https://weaveos.com/methodology/ai-roi) before interpreting an output ratio as ROI.
